consensus_summary: A disciple is a committed follower and learner of Jesus, generally understood by the majority as synonymous with any Christian believer, characterized by obedience, love, and cross-bearing.
book_summary: A disciple is one in whom the covenant law is sealed, who meets the strict exclusionary conditions of forsaking all and cross-bearing, and is perfected to carry the Name and Word of the Master.
consensus_core_identification: A learner and follower of Jesus Christ.
book_core_identification: One in whom the law is sealed, who proves it by continuing in the word, and who fulfills the strict conditions of cross-bearing and forsaking all.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus generally extends the term to all Christian believers, while the book restricts it to a subset of believers who demonstrably meet the absolute conditions of Luke 14 (forsaking all, bearing the cross) and have the covenant law sealed in them.
material_contradiction: The book rejects the 'commonly taught' view that any believer entered by faith and baptism is inherently a disciple, instead enforcing Jesus' three 'cannots' in Luke 14 as strict boundaries for the title.
rationale: The book builds upon the same core texts as the consensus (Luke 14, John 8) but refines the concept by treating the demanding conditions of discipleship as definitive, exclusionary boundaries rather than general characteristics. It also adds a covenantal dimension (Isaiah 8:16) not emphasized in the consensus.
strongest_objection: Acts 11:26 states that 'the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch,' which heavily implies that 'disciple' was the standard, synonymous designation for any member of the church, rather than a restricted class of those who had reached a specific level of perfection or forsaking all.
